But if you're just standing on the sidewalk, and you don't have anywhere to be, and you don't even care if a bus ever drives down that street again... you're not hopeless. You're just standing there. turns.doctor_question: During these past 14 months, have you felt worthless?
turns.patient_response:
Worthless? No, I wouldn't use that word. I don't feel worthless. I mean, I know my situation right now isn't exactly... ideal. Being suspended from the site, sitting in my apartment all day in my Hanes t-shirts, not having the radio to listen to the dispatch calls anymore. It's frustrating, absolutely. It feels like I've been sidelined, like I was put on the bench right when I was starting to figure out some of the deeper security protocols they were implementing downtown. 

But worthless implies that I have no value, or that I don't serve a purpose, and I know that's not true. I still have my bachelor's degree, which I worked incredibly hard for. I still have all the training and the observational skills I developed over the years on the job. Just because they took my uniform and told me to stay home doesn't erase what's in my head, you know? I'm still the same person who knows how to secure a perimeter and spot anomalies in a crowd. 

I might not be actively utilizing those skills on a payroll right this second, but that doesn't mean the skills themselves are worthless, and it certainly doesn't mean I am. I'm just... I'm in a holding pattern. Like an airplane circling the airport waiting for clearance to land. The plane isn't worthless just because it's not on the tarmac, right? It's just waiting. That's how I look at it. I'm just waiting for this suspension nonsense to get cleared up so I can get back to doing what I do best. So no, I don't sit around feeling worthless or like I don't matter. I just feel like I'm on pause.

symptom_reasoning.S030: The patient explicitly states they do not feel worthless and believe they still have value and purpose.
symptom_reasoning.S042: The patient denies feeling incompetent or worthless, emphasizing their skills, training, and degree.

turns.doctor_question: During these past 14 months, have you yourself felt slowed down in your movements, speech, or thinking?
turns.patient_response:
Slowed down? No, no, I haven't felt slowed down at all. If anything, my mind is moving just as fast as it always has, maybe even faster. I mean, thinking-wise, I'm constantly analyzing everything around me. Even when I'm just sitting in my apartment, like I said, watching those old detective shows or looking out the window, my brain is firing on all cylinders. I'm tracking the people walking by on the sidewalk, noting what kind of cars are parked on the street, checking if the streetlights are flickering in any kind of pattern. You have to stay sharp, you know? You can't let your guard down just because you're off the clock. 

And my movements, no, they're perfectly normal. I walk at my usual pace. When I go down to the laundromat on Sundays, I'm not dragging my feet or shuffling along like an old man. I have a very deliberate stride. It's a purposeful walk. In security, you learn how to walk with authority, even when you don't have the uniform on. You keep your shoulders back, your head on a swivel, scanning the environment. I still do that. I can get from my front door to the laundromat in exactly four minutes and thirty seconds if I hit the crosswalk right at Elm Street. I've timed it. 

As for my speech, well, you can hear me right now. I'm not slurring my words, I'm not taking long pauses to figure out what I want to say. I know exactly what I want to say, and I say it. I've always been a clear communicator. When you're calling in a report to dispatch, you have to be concise, you have to enunciate, you have to make sure every single detail is transmitted clearly over the radio because if there's static or interference, they might miss a crucial piece of information. I carry that over into my everyday life. So no, I haven't noticed any slowing down in my thinking, my walking, my talking... none of it. I'm completely up to speed.

turns.doctor_question: Because of these symptoms, are you unable to work at all right now?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's not that I'm unable to work. Like I was saying before about being in a holding pattern, my skills are completely intact. I am fully capable of working. But... I am not currently working, no. I got suspended from my protective service job. 

And the whole thing was completely overblown, if you ask me. Let me explain exactly how that went down, because it's important context. I was just doing a routine patrol through the main concourse—Section 4, right near the west entrance. I was executing my perimeter checks exactly how we were trained, observing the crowd dynamics, looking for anything out of place. But apparently, my methods... well, management pulled me into the office and told me I had scared some of the retail staff and a few of the bystanders. They said I was being too intense, asking too many questions about who was watching the exits and checking people's bags. I was just trying to secure the area, making sure everything was locked down, but they didn't see it that way. They took my badge, took my radio, and put me on this indefinite suspension. 

And since that happened... I don't know, it just threw my whole schedule off track. It's not just the job that stopped. I used to be really involved in a lot of things outside of work. I was coaching a youth basketball league on Thursday nights down at the community rec center—the 10-to-12-year-old bracket. I had this whole defensive playbook mapped out for the kids, taught them how to watch the opponent's hips to predict their movements. And I used to volunteer on Saturday mornings helping sort out the logistics at the local food pantry. 

But after the suspension came down... I just stopped going. I pulled away from all of it. The coaching, the volunteering... I haven't been back to the rec center in months. I haven't answered calls from the other coaches or the pantry coordinator. I've basically just pulled away from most of the people who used to count on me. It's just... it's easier to stay in the apartment right now. I don't want to have to explain the suspension to everybody, and honestly, I need to be here, keeping an eye on things from my window, staying sharp until this whole misunderstanding at work gets resolved and they put me back on the roster. So yeah, I'm not working, but it's not because I can't. It's just how things have played out.

symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient describes a marked loss of interest and participation in previously enjoyed activities, such as coaching youth basketball and volunteering at a food pantry.

symptom_reasoning.S079: The patient exhibits sustained alertness and safety checking, describing intense perimeter checks at work that scared others, and currently staying in their apartment to 'keep an eye on things from my window, staying sharp'.

turns.doctor_question: When you hear those transmissions, are they happening only during the times you feel that empty loss of interest, or do they also happen when your mood feels normal?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... it's not like they only happen when I'm feeling that sort of... that empty feeling, you know, the loss of interest in everything. It's not tied to that. I mean, they happen regardless of how I'm feeling. Even on days when I wake up and I feel completely normal, like I'm ready to get back on the job, I'll still get those transmissions. 

Like last Tuesday, for example. I woke up, had my coffee—black, two sugars, just like always—and I felt fine. I felt sharp. I was reviewing some old incident reports I kept from my training days, just brushing up on protocol, and I felt completely engaged. My mood was perfectly normal. And right in the middle of reading a report on crowd control tactics, I heard it. Clear as day. A transmission coming through the scanner, even though the battery was sitting right there on the kitchen table next to my mug. 

It was a male voice, very authoritative, like a dispatcher, giving out coordinates. Alpha-Tango-Niner, something like that. I grabbed my notebook right away to log it. I always keep a notebook handy. You never know when you'll need to document something. So I'm writing down the time—it was exactly 0945 hours—and the exact phrasing of the transmission, and I'm feeling completely alert, completely focused. There was no emptiness, no loss of interest. I was fully dialed in. 

And then there are other times, like when I'm just sitting by the window, feeling kind of... detached, I guess you could say. When I'm just watching the streetlights and I don't really care about the basketball league or the food pantry or any of it. Even then, the transmissions still come through. It's like they're on a completely different frequency from my mood, if that makes sense. They're independent variables. 

So yeah, to answer your question, they happen all the time. Whether I'm feeling normal and ready for duty, or whether I'm stuck in that holding pattern feeling empty, the scanner still picks up those signals. It's constant monitoring, really. You just have to be ready to log the data whenever it comes in, regardless of how you're feeling at that particular moment.

turns.doctor_question: Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing those transmissions even though you were not feeling empty or uninterested at all?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, definitely. Like I was just saying, there have absolutely been stretches—two weeks, three weeks, even longer—where my mood was completely fine, totally stable, no emptiness at all, and I was still getting the transmissions. The transmissions don't care about my mood. They operate on their own schedule. 

And, you know, I should probably clarify exactly what I'm hearing, because it's not just random static or coordinates like I mentioned before. I mean, sometimes it's coordinates, but a lot of the time, the voices coming through the scanner—these short, very clipped, radio-like voices—they're giving me tactical updates. Warnings, really. Like, I'll be sitting there, feeling totally normal, maybe eating a sandwich, and the scanner will crackle, even with the battery out, and a voice will say, "Perimeter breached, hostiles inside," or "Subject is under surveillance." It's very specific, very urgent. It's telling me someone is inside my apartment or that I'm being watched from the outside. 

And that's... well, that's why I have to stay so vigilant, you see? Because it's not just the audio. It's visual, too. I'll hear that warning, that someone is inside, and I'll immediately initiate a full sweep of the apartment. I check the closets, under the bed, behind the shower curtain—standard clearing procedures. I make sure every single room is secure. But even after I've cleared the entire perimeter, and I know for a fact the doors are deadbolted, I'll still see it. A shadow. Just... darting past the hallway out of the corner of my eye. 

It's incredibly fast, like someone moving with extreme tactical precision, trying to evade detection. I'll sweep the area again, obviously, because you can't just ignore a visual confirmation after receiving an audio warning, but I never catch them. They're too quick. But the point is, all of this—the radio voices warning me, the shadows in the hallway—this happens all the time. It happens when I'm feeling empty, sure, but it absolutely happens for weeks at a time when I'm feeling completely normal, completely focused, and just trying to maintain my readiness. The phenomena are completely independent of my emotional state, doctor. They are external variables that I just have to constantly monitor and manage.
